title: What’s the best AI tool or plan for turning a 2D image into a 3D model as a complete beginner?
author: Entire_Nectarine8291
selftext:
**What’s the best deal right now?** If you were starting today, which AI tool or plan would you try? If you’ve paid for one, how much did you pay, how many attempts did you get, and could you export the mesh to work on it later?

**What advice would you give a complete beginner?** I’ve never used Blender, worked with 3D character models, or rigged anything for animation. I do have some experience with CAD and SolidWorks, if that helps at all. Any advice on where to start would be appreciated.

I mainly want to turn 2D character designs into 3D models, but I’d also like to try making buildings and other objects.

**Two smaller questions**  
I’ve seen some posts about Black Friday deals. Are these actually the best prices you’ve seen in the last three or four months, or are these the usual prices dressed up as Black Friday deals?

Tripo AI is the tool I see mentioned most often (I’ve heard it’s the best for making characters, which is why I’m asking about it specifically). Its ads look a lot better than the models I see on its Explore page. If you’ve used it for characters, are results like the ones in the ads realistic, or are those examples cherry-picked or cleaned up afterward?

comments.author: Embergloam
comments.body:
Just did this with a gnome sorcerer for a 3D prototype. Claude Code drove the whole thing... wrote the scripts, hit the Meshy and Tripo APIs, and even rigged and animated in Blender with no UI open. I mostly picked images and complained about runs.

I was only mucking around with a prototype so I didn't spend a lot of time futzing with it. Lighting then fixed up the rest to where it felt quite close to the original concept.

\--- here's a general summary of events / findings ---

**Concept:** all local, Z-Image Turbo in ComfyUI. Free, so we just ran rounds of mood art until one clicked. The vibe I wanted was "cute but also serious and whimsical": old gnome, patched violet robe, brass trinkets, goggles on a crooked hat. Stuff I learned:

* Typing "A-pose" does nothing. "Both arms held out to the sides and angled down at forty-five degrees, palms down" works.
* Style words matter a lot. "Chunky storybook" gave me a garden gnome. A painterly character style fixed it.
* I asked for a small nose like five different ways and kept getting a round red bulb.

**Sheet + views:** Meshy image-to-image (nano-banana) redraws your favorite concept into a clean front A-pose, then makes matching back and side views. 3 credits a pop, really good. Gotcha: every view comes back with slivers of the neighboring view on its edges. Crop them off, or the 3D gen builds junk out of them.

**Meshy vs Tripo:** my spouse swore by Tripo so I gave it a shot, fed both the same four images. Meshy's gnome came out a caricature, big nose and scowl, and it squashed the tall hat into a beanie. Tripo kept the hat, gave a softer face closer to the concept, half the file size, and a 78-bone rig with fingers and eye bones. The idle and run just had more personality. Not close. Meshy still does the views; Tripo does the model and rig. Big lesson: the 3D face comes straight from your concept, so fix the face in 2D first.

**Pain points:**

* **Eyes are painted into the texture, no face rig.** We tried projecting live blinking eyes onto the head and it was genuinely terrifying. Nope.
* **Long robes get skinned to the legs.** Go knee-length.
* **Stock runs.** Every preset is human motion, and on a three-and-a-half-foot gnome the strides are tiny. To hit our game's run speed you play them 4–8x fast and it's super fast speedwalking. Mixamo was meh, AI text-to-motion runs looked like he'd hurt his ankle, and about eight rounds of building the run procedurally in three.js never felt alive.
* **What worked:** Claude scripting Blender directly. IK legs, foot paths on the ground, a forward surge in the pelvis, overlap on the spine, head and arms. I gave it notes like I'd give an animator: springy, real airtime, never floaty, closed fists, exaggerate the arcs because short limbs don't read at distance. Classic WoW gnome run as the feel reference. Then live sliders in the browser so I could tune it myself. It can't judge feel from screenshots, but I can.
* **Four-legged creatures:** Tripo's quadruped rig ate the forelegs on a fluffy ram twice, so Claude built that rig from scratch in Blender too.

https://i.redd.it/onpc2kvik84i1.jpeg

**Cost:** about 115 Meshy credits and about 160 Tripo credits for all the gnome experiments. The animation was the real time sink, not the model.

replies.author: Entire_Nectarine8291
replies.body:
Basic questions,

can I just use ChatGPT/gemini for image concepts? I like Z image Turbo, but I never do better than the big model ones.

Same with Meshy? Why not use GPT/Gemini for the character sheet?

You have the animation so I can see? Would love to see the results of your workflow!

And Claude (I assume with MCP, another person told me this, I got no idea what it means) makes the animation

replies.author: Embergloam
replies.body:
You can, yeah - but you can also just ask your agents to use them as well. I'm not going into ComfyUI myself anymore and prompting; I have Claude doing all of it, and it just sends me the generations the prompt resulted in.

For Meshy: you can use GPT/Gemini for the character sheet, and I kind of did - Meshy's image-to-image runs on Nano Banana (Gemini's image model), so I used it to redraw my favorite concept as a clean front A-pose sheet, then had Meshy generate the side and back views. GPT/Gemini stop at flat images though. The 3D model, rig and animations need something like Meshy or Tripo. I tried both and Tripo won on the character itself.

RE: MCP, probably the best analogy is "USB for AI" -- before USB existed, every printer/mouse/camera/etc needed its own special port and driver. USB made one standard plug so pretty much any device works with any computer. MCP ("Model Context Protocol") does that same job for AI assistants: one standard way to "plug" an AI into outside tools and data like Google Drive, calendars, etc.

There are APIs too, which each service designs on its own - Google Drive has its own API, Slack has another, etc. MCP is a kind of wrapper that sits on top of those APIs and is built so an AI can use them. Put another way: an API is a restaurant's kitchen window, where each restaurant has its own menu and its own way to order. MCP is a waiter who speaks one language to the AI. The waiter hands it a menu it can read, takes its order, and passes it to whichever kitchen it needs.

My setup doesn't actually use MCP at all. Claude writes small scripts that call ComfyUI's, Meshy's and Tripo's APIs directly. For the animation, none of the stock or generated runs felt right, so Claude drove Blender with a Python script and keyed the run cycle to my notes, then exported it into the game. That's the API vs MCP thing in practice: MCP is great for one-off "go do X" requests, but for a pipeline you run over and over, scripts hitting the APIs are faster and cheaper.

comments.author: Quirky-Map1995
comments.body: If you are just starting without any prior experience, Id recommended skipping 3d generated meshes all together at start and use public CC0 assets from stuff like polyhaven And polypizza and use them for prototyping and once u get the hang of it slowly upgrade them, will be much easier to understand that u cant put meshes with 5 mil+ triangles into game and then u can try to utilize stuff like tripo with smart topology even tho its not best and game its good starting point for most meshes
